lessons.title: Alkenes, alcohols and carboxylic acids
lessons.summary: Meet three more families of carbon compounds: the reactive alkenes with their double bonds, the alcohols found in drinks and fuels, and the carboxylic acids that give vinegar its sharpness.
objectives: I can name and draw the first four alkenes and explain why they are unsaturated.
I can describe the reactions of alkenes with hydrogen, water and the halogens.
I can name and draw the first four alcohols and describe their reactions and uses.
I can describe how ethanol is made by fermentation.
I can name the first four carboxylic acids and explain why they are weak acids.

activities.title: Alkenes and the double bond
activities.content:
## A second family of hydrocarbons

The **alkenes** are hydrocarbons that contain a **carbon–carbon double bond, C=C**. Because of the double bond, an alkene has two fewer hydrogen atoms than the alkane with the same number of carbons.

General formula: **CₙH₂ₙ**

| Name | Formula | Structure |
|---|---|---|
| ethene | C₂H₄ | CH₂=CH₂ |
| propene | C₃H₆ | CH₂=CH–CH₃ |
| butene | C₄H₈ | CH₂=CH–CH₂–CH₃ |
| pentene | C₅H₁₀ | CH₂=CH–CH₂–CH₂–CH₃ |

The names all end in **-ene**. The C=C group is called a **functional group**: it is the part of the molecule that does the reacting, so all alkenes behave in a similar way. A group of compounds with the same functional group is a **homologous series**.

### Saturated and unsaturated

Alkanes have only single bonds and are **saturated**: every carbon has as many hydrogens as it can hold. Alkenes are **unsaturated** because the double bond could open up to accept more atoms.

### Burning alkenes

Alkenes burn in air, but with a **smokier flame** than alkanes because they tend to burn incompletely, producing carbon (soot) and carbon monoxide as well as carbon dioxide and water.

activities.title: Worked example: the bromine water test
activities.content:
**How can you tell hexane from hexene? They are both colourless liquids.**

Add a few drops of **bromine water** (orange) to each and shake.

- **Hexane** (an alkane): the mixture **stays orange**. Nothing happens, because there is no double bond to react.
- **Hexene** (an alkene): the mixture turns **colourless**. The bromine has added across the double bond to form dibromohexane, which has no colour.

This is the standard test for an alkene. The key phrase to write in the exam is: **"bromine water changes from orange to colourless"**. Do not say "clear", because a coloured solution can also be clear.

**What is happening?**

C₆H₁₂ + Br₂ → C₆H₁₂Br₂

The double bond breaks open and each carbon that was in the double bond gains a bromine atom. This is an **addition reaction**: two molecules join to make one, with nothing left over.

question.text: Which of these is the molecular formula of the alkene with four carbon atoms?
question.explanation: Butene has n = 4, so the formula is C₄H₈. C₄H₁₀ is butane, the alkane.

options.feedback: That is butane, an alkane with only single bonds.

activities.title: Addition reactions of alkenes
activities.content:
## Opening the double bond

Because the C=C bond can open up, alkenes take part in **addition reactions**. Three are on the specification.

### 1. Hydrogen (hydrogenation)

ethene + hydrogen → ethane

C₂H₄ + H₂ → C₂H₆

Conditions: a **nickel catalyst** and about 150 °C. The alkene becomes a saturated alkane. This is used to harden vegetable oils into margarine.

### 2. Water (hydration)

ethene + steam → ethanol

C₂H₄ + H₂O → C₂H₅OH

Conditions: **steam**, high temperature and pressure, and a **catalyst** (phosphoric acid). This is one of the two ways ethanol is made industrially.

### 3. Halogens

ethene + bromine → dibromoethane

C₂H₄ + Br₂ → C₂H₄Br₂

Chlorine and iodine react in the same way. No catalyst is needed. The product has a halogen atom on each of the two carbons that were double bonded.

### Drawing the products

When you draw the product, the double bond becomes a single bond and the two new atoms sit on the neighbouring carbons:

```
  H   H            H   H
   \ /             |   |
    C=C   + Br₂ →  H-C-C-H
   / \             |   |
  H   H            Br  Br
```

activities.title: Worked example: propene plus hydrogen
activities.content:
**Write the equation for propene reacting with hydrogen, and name the product.**

Propene is C₃H₆ with structure CH₂=CH–CH₃.

Hydrogen adds across the double bond: one H goes on each of the two double-bonded carbons.

C₃H₆ + H₂ → C₃H₈

The product has only single bonds and three carbons, so it is **propane**.

**Now propene plus chlorine.**

C₃H₆ + Cl₂ → C₃H₆Cl₂

The product is **dichloropropane**. Each Cl sits on one of the carbons that were in the double bond.

**And propene plus steam.**

C₃H₆ + H₂O → C₃H₇OH

The product is **propanol**, an alcohol. The –OH goes on one carbon and the –H on the other.

**Pattern:** the alkene's carbon skeleton stays the same; only the double bond changes.

question.text: Match each reaction of ethene to its product.
question.hint: Hydrogen gives an alkane, steam gives an alcohol, bromine gives a dibromo compound.
question.explanation: Ethene + H₂ → ethane (hydrogenation). Ethene + H₂O → ethanol (hydration). Ethene + Br₂ → dibromoethane.

activities.title: Alcohols
activities.content:
## The –OH functional group

**Alcohols** contain the **hydroxyl group, –OH**, attached to a carbon chain. Their names end in **-ol**.

| Name | Formula | Structure |
|---|---|---|
| methanol | CH₃OH | CH₃–OH |
| ethanol | C₂H₅OH | CH₃–CH₂–OH |
| propanol | C₃H₇OH | CH₃–CH₂–CH₂–OH |
| butanol | C₄H₉OH | CH₃–CH₂–CH₂–CH₂–OH |

### Properties and reactions

- **Dissolve in water** to give a **neutral** solution (pH 7).
- **Burn** in air to form carbon dioxide and water: C₂H₅OH + 3O₂ → 2CO₂ + 3H₂O. This makes ethanol a useful **fuel**.
- **React with sodium** to give hydrogen gas and a compound called sodium ethoxide. The reaction is gentler than sodium with water.
- Can be **oxidised** to **carboxylic acids**. Ethanol is oxidised to ethanoic acid using an oxidising agent, or slowly by bacteria in the air, which is why open wine turns to vinegar.

### Uses

Ethanol is used as a **solvent** (in perfumes and marker pens), as a **fuel** (on its own or blended with petrol), and in **alcoholic drinks**. Methanol is a solvent and a chemical feedstock.

### Making ethanol by fermentation

Yeast converts sugar (glucose) to ethanol and carbon dioxide:

C₆H₁₂O₆ → 2C₂H₅OH + 2CO₂

Conditions: about **30–40 °C**, **no oxygen** (anaerobic), and **yeast** to provide the enzymes. Too cold and the enzymes work slowly; too hot and they are destroyed.

metadata.blanksText: In fermentation, ___ provides enzymes that convert glucose into ethanol and ___ gas. The mixture is kept warm at about 35 °C and air is kept out because the process needs ___ conditions.

question.hint: The living organism used is a fungus; the gas is the one that makes bread rise; no oxygen is another way of saying the last word.
question.explanation: Yeast converts glucose to ethanol and carbon dioxide under anaerobic (oxygen-free) conditions.

activities.title: Worked example: fermentation or hydration?
activities.content:
**A company wants to make ethanol. Compare the two methods.**

| | Fermentation | Hydration of ethene |
|---|---|---|
| Raw material | sugar from plants (renewable) | ethene from crude oil (non-renewable) |
| Conditions | 30–40 °C, atmospheric pressure | high temperature and pressure, catalyst |
| Speed | slow (days) | fast, continuous |
| Product | dilute ethanol that must be distilled | pure ethanol |
| Energy use | low | high |

**Which is better?** It depends on what matters. Fermentation uses a renewable resource and mild conditions, so it is more sustainable and is used for drinks and bio-fuel. Hydration is faster and gives pure ethanol, so it is preferred where large amounts of pure ethanol are needed for industry and cheap ethene is available.

When an exam asks you to compare, give **at least one point from each side** and then say which you would choose **and why**.

question.text: Which statements about ethanol are correct? Select all that apply.
question.hint: Think about pH, what it burns to, and what it is oxidised to.
question.explanation: Ethanol solutions are neutral, and ethanol burns to form carbon dioxide and water. Oxidising ethanol gives ethanoic acid, not ethene, and ethanol reacts with sodium to give hydrogen, not oxygen.

options.text: A solution of ethanol in water has a pH of about 7.
Ethanol burns to produce carbon dioxide and water.
Ethanol is oxidised to form ethene.
Ethanol reacts with sodium to give oxygen gas.

activities.title: Carboxylic acids
activities.content:
## The –COOH functional group

**Carboxylic acids** contain the **carboxyl group, –COOH**. Their names end in **-oic acid**.

| Name | Formula | Found in |
|---|---|---|
| methanoic acid | HCOOH | ant stings |
| ethanoic acid | CH₃COOH | vinegar |
| propanoic acid | C₂H₅COOH | food preservative |
| butanoic acid | C₃H₇COOH | rancid butter |

### Reactions

Carboxylic acids behave like other acids, just more gently:

- **Dissolve in water** to give an **acidic** solution (pH about 3).
- **React with carbonates** to give a salt, water and carbon dioxide, so they **fizz** with sodium carbonate. The salt from ethanoic acid is called an **ethanoate**: e.g. sodium ethanoate.
- **React with alcohols**, in the presence of an acid catalyst, to make **esters**. Ethanoic acid + ethanol → ethyl ethanoate + water. Esters have sweet, fruity smells and are used in flavourings and perfumes.

### Why are they weak acids? (Higher)

A strong acid such as hydrochloric acid is **fully ionised** in water. Ethanoic acid is only **partially ionised**: most molecules stay as CH₃COOH and only a few release H⁺.

CH₃COOH ⇌ CH₃COO⁻ + H⁺

So at the same concentration a carboxylic acid has **fewer H⁺ ions** and a **higher pH** than a strong acid, and reacts more slowly with metals and carbonates.

question.text: Put these stages in order to show how ethanoic acid in vinegar can be made starting from sugar.
question.hint: Sugar becomes ethanol first; then the ethanol is changed into the acid.
question.explanation: Glucose is fermented by yeast to ethanol; the ethanol is then oxidised (by bacteria in air, or an oxidising agent) to ethanoic acid.
order: Dissolve glucose in water and add yeast
Keep warm without oxygen so fermentation produces ethanol
Oxidise the ethanol using air or an oxidising agent

question.text:
A student has three unlabelled colourless liquids: butane (a liquefied gas), butene and butanol.

(a) Describe a test to identify the butene, and give the result.

(b) Explain why butene reacts in this test but butane does not.

(c) The student burns some butanol. Write the word equation for its complete combustion.

(d) **Higher tier:** Butanol can be oxidised to butanoic acid. Explain why a solution of butanoic acid has a higher pH than hydrochloric acid of the same concentration.
question.hint: The alkene test uses an orange solution. The alcohol burns like any fuel. Think about how much of a weak acid ionises.
question.explanation: (a) Add bromine water and shake: with butene it turns from orange to colourless. (b) Butene has a C=C double bond (it is unsaturated) so bromine can add across it; butane is saturated with only single bonds. (c) butanol + oxygen → carbon dioxide + water. (d) Butanoic acid is a weak acid and only partially ionises, so it produces fewer H⁺ ions than hydrochloric acid, which is fully ionised.

markScheme.criterion: Add bromine water; it turns from orange to colourless with butene
Butene has a C=C double bond / is unsaturated, so an addition reaction occurs; butane is saturated
Word equation: butanol + oxygen → carbon dioxide + water
Butanoic acid is a weak acid / only partially ionised
So it has a lower concentration of H⁺ ions than the fully ionised hydrochloric acid

activities.title: Key points
activities.content:
- **Alkenes** CₙH₂ₙ have a **C=C double bond** and are **unsaturated**. Test: **bromine water turns from orange to colourless**.
- Alkenes undergo **addition** with **hydrogen** (→ alkane, nickel catalyst), **steam** (→ alcohol, catalyst) and **halogens** (→ dihalogenoalkane). They burn with a smoky flame.
- **Alcohols** contain **–OH** and end in **-ol**: methanol, ethanol, propanol, butanol. Neutral in water, burn to CO₂ + H₂O, react with sodium to give H₂, oxidise to carboxylic acids.
- **Fermentation**: glucose → ethanol + CO₂ with yeast, ~35 °C, anaerobic. Or ethanol from ethene + steam.
- **Carboxylic acids** contain **–COOH** and end in **-oic acid**: methanoic, ethanoic, propanoic, butanoic. Acidic, fizz with carbonates, form **esters** with alcohols.
- Higher: carboxylic acids are **weak** because they only **partially ionise** in water.

practiceQuestions.text: What is the functional group in an alcohol?

options.feedback: That is the alkene functional group.
That is the carboxylic acid functional group.

practiceQuestions.text: True or false: alkenes are described as saturated hydrocarbons.
practiceQuestions.hint: What does the double bond allow the molecule to do?
practiceQuestions.explanation: False. Alkenes contain a C=C double bond and are unsaturated. Alkanes are saturated.

practiceQuestions.text: Complete the equation for the addition of hydrogen to ethene.

metadata.blanksText: C₂H₄ + H₂ → ___ , and the product is called ___.

practiceQuestions.hint: Add two hydrogens to the formula of ethene; the product is an alkane with two carbons.
practiceQuestions.explanation: C₂H₄ + H₂ → C₂H₆, which is ethane.

practiceQuestions.text: Which compound is a carboxylic acid?
practiceQuestions.hint: Look for the –COOH group in the formula.
practiceQuestions.explanation: CH₃COOH is ethanoic acid. C₂H₅OH is ethanol, C₂H₄ is ethene and C₃H₈ is propane.

practiceQuestions.text: Using the general formula for alkenes, how many hydrogen atoms are there in a molecule of the alkene with 7 carbon atoms?
Match each compound to the homologous series it belongs to.
practiceQuestions.hint: Look at the ending of each name.
practiceQuestions.explanation: Propene ends in -ene (alkene); propanol ends in -ol (alcohol); propanoic acid ends in -oic acid (carboxylic acid).

practiceQuestions.text: Ethanol burns according to C₂H₅OH + 3O₂ → 2CO₂ + 3H₂O. Calculate the mass of carbon dioxide, in grams, produced when 9.2 g of ethanol burns completely. (Mr: C₂H₅OH = 46, CO₂ = 44)
practiceQuestions.hint: Find moles of ethanol, use the 1 : 2 ratio, then multiply by 44.
practiceQuestions.explanation: moles ethanol = 9.2 ÷ 46 = 0.2 mol. Moles CO₂ = 0.4 mol. mass = 0.4 × 44 = 17.6 g.

practiceQuestions.text: Which observations would you expect when a small piece of sodium is added to ethanol? Select all that apply.
practiceQuestions.hint: Compare it with sodium in water, but calmer.
practiceQuestions.explanation: Sodium reacts with ethanol to produce hydrogen gas (bubbles) and sodium ethoxide; the reaction is steady, not violent, and there is no colour change to purple.

options.text: Bubbles of hydrogen gas are produced.
The sodium slowly gets smaller as it reacts.
The reaction is more violent than sodium with water.
options.feedback: It is less vigorous than the reaction with water.

practiceQuestions.text: Describe how ethanol is produced by fermentation. Include the raw material, the conditions needed and the products.
practiceQuestions.explanation: Sugar (glucose) solution is mixed with yeast and kept warm at about 30–40 °C with no oxygen present. Enzymes in the yeast convert the glucose into ethanol and carbon dioxide.

practiceQuestions.text:
Ethanoic acid is found in vinegar.

(a) Give the formula of ethanoic acid.

(b) A student adds sodium carbonate to ethanoic acid. Describe what is observed and name the gas produced.

(c) Name the type of compound formed when ethanoic acid reacts with ethanol, and describe one property of these compounds.
practiceQuestions.hint: The formula contains the –COOH group. Carbonates and acids always give the same gas. Acid + alcohol gives a sweet-smelling compound.
practiceQuestions.explanation: (a) CH₃COOH. (b) Fizzing / bubbles as carbon dioxide gas is given off. (c) An ester (ethyl ethanoate), which has a sweet, fruity smell and is used in flavourings and perfumes.

markScheme.criterion: Ester formed; sweet or fruity smell / used in perfumes and flavourings

practiceQuestions.text: Propene is the alkene that contains three carbon atoms. Which of these is its molecular formula?
practiceQuestions.hint: Alkenes fit the general formula CₙH₂ₙ. Put n = 3.
practiceQuestions.explanation: For an alkene with n = 3, the number of hydrogens is 2 × 3 = 6, so propene is C₃H₆. C₃H₈ is propane, the alkane with the same number of carbons.

options.feedback: That is propane, the saturated alkane.

practiceQuestions.text: Propene, C₃H₆, takes part in the same addition reactions as ethene. Match each reaction of propene to its product.
practiceQuestions.hint: Adding hydrogen gives the alkane, adding steam gives the alcohol, and adding bromine gives a compound with two bromine atoms.
practiceQuestions.explanation: Propene + H₂ → propane (hydrogenation). Propene + H₂O → propanol (hydration). Propene + Br₂ → dibromopropane. In each case the double bond opens and the new atoms add across it.

practiceQuestions.text: Complete the sentences about the conditions used in fermentation.

metadata.blanksText: Fermentation is carried out at about 35 °C. If the temperature is much higher, the ___ in the yeast are denatured and stop working; if it is much lower, the reaction becomes too ___. Air is kept out of the vessel because oxygen would allow the ethanol to be oxidised to ___ acid.

practiceQuestions.hint: Yeast contains biological catalysts. Think about how the rate changes when it is cold. The acid formed is the one found in vinegar.
practiceQuestions.explanation: Yeast works because of its enzymes, which are denatured if too hot. Below the optimum temperature the fermentation is too slow. Oxygen must be excluded because it oxidises ethanol to ethanoic acid (the acid in vinegar).

practiceQuestions.text: Propanol, C₃H₇OH, is an alcohol. Which statements about propanol are correct? Select all that apply.
practiceQuestions.hint: Alcohols behave like ethanol: think about pH, burning, and whether they contain a double bond.
practiceQuestions.explanation: Propanol dissolves in water to give a neutral solution (pH about 7) and burns completely to give carbon dioxide and water. It is not an acid, so it does not fizz with sodium carbonate, and it has no C=C double bond, so bromine water stays orange.

options.text: Propanol dissolves in water to give a solution with a pH of about 7.
Propanol burns in air to form carbon dioxide and water.
Propanol fizzes when added to sodium carbonate.
options.feedback: Only carboxylic acids react with carbonates; propanol is not an acid.
Propanol has no C=C double bond, so bromine water stays orange.

practiceQuestions.text: Put these stages in order to show how ethanol can be made industrially starting from crude oil.
practiceQuestions.hint: Crude oil must be separated first, then a long-chain fraction is broken down to make the alkene needed.
practiceQuestions.explanation: Crude oil is separated into fractions by fractional distillation; a long-chain fraction is cracked to produce ethene; ethene is then hydrated by reacting it with steam over a catalyst to form ethanol.
order: Separate crude oil into fractions by fractional distillation
Crack a long-chain fraction to produce ethene
React ethene with steam at high temperature over a catalyst

practiceQuestions.text:
A technician has three unlabelled colourless liquids: pentane, pentene and a solution of pentanoic acid.

(a) Describe a test the technician could use to identify the pentene, and give the result.

(b) Explain why pentene gives this result but pentane does not.

(c) Describe a test using sodium carbonate that would identify the pentanoic acid solution, and give the observation.

(d) **Higher tier:** Explain why a solution of pentanoic acid has a higher pH than a solution of hydrochloric acid of the same concentration.
practiceQuestions.hint: An orange solution identifies alkenes. Carboxylic acids react with carbonates like any acid. Compare how completely a weak acid and a strong acid ionise.
practiceQuestions.explanation: (a) Shake each liquid with bromine water; pentene turns it from orange to colourless. (b) Pentene contains a C=C double bond (it is unsaturated), so bromine can add across the double bond; pentane is saturated and has no double bond. (c) Add sodium carbonate: the pentanoic acid fizzes because carbon dioxide gas is released. (d) Pentanoic acid is a weak acid, so only a small fraction of its molecules ionise to release H⁺ ions; hydrochloric acid is a strong acid that is fully ionised, so it has a higher concentration of H⁺ ions and a lower pH.

markScheme.criterion: Add bromine water; with pentene it turns from orange to colourless
Pentene has a C=C double bond / is unsaturated so addition occurs; pentane is saturated
Pentanoic acid fizzes / bubbles of carbon dioxide with sodium carbonate
Pentanoic acid is a weak acid / only partially ionised
So it has fewer H⁺ ions than the fully ionised (strong) hydrochloric acid
